strengths: The motivation for this work is strong - being able to train policies entirely offline that are then able to be deployed with safety guarantees in the real environment would significantly advance the applicability of RL to real-world scenarios
The novelty is good - this is a new method which combines DT with Lyapunov conditioning
The authors compare against many baseline methods on several different tasks

The idea of prompting a world model using self-generated trajectories is interesting and promising. Experimental results also show that the idea indeed improves the agent's test-time performance in some tasks.

In this work, the author presents a simple model-based RL method with a transformer and a world model and proposes a Lyapunov-conditioned self-alignment method, which does not require retraining and conducts the test-time adaptation for the desired criteria. The author shows that the model-based RL with the transformer architecture can be described as a model-based hierarchical RL. As a result, the author can combine hierarchical RL and in-context learning for self-alignment in transformers. The proposed self-alignment framework aims to make the agent safe by self-instructing with the Lyapunov condition. In experiments, the author demonstrates that the self-alignment algorithm outperforms safe RL methods in continuous control and safe RL benchmark environments in terms of return, costs, and failure rate. This paper is largely well-organized and clear in its presentation.
weaknesses: The training procedure for the DT+VAE model is not provided; it is unclear how the VAE is trained in conjunction with the Decision Transformer, what loss function is used for the VAE decoder, how this loss is combined with the DT loss, and the specific architecture of the VAE is not described, making reproduction difficult.

The authors mention "sampling policies" (lines 245-256) but it is unclear where policies are sampled in Algorithm 1, how imagined trajectories relate to specific policies, and how those policies are parameterized or sampled from a distribution.

It is not clear how the results in Section 4, specifically the derivation of the control invariant set and the threshold D, are used in Algorithm 1; the connection between the theoretical results and the practical implementation is missing.

It is not clear how the maximization in equation 8 is performed; the relationship between the two loops in Algorithm 1 and the maximization of U and V needs clarification regarding joint or sequential optimization.

The roles of θ and ψ in the architecture are unclear; it is not explained how these parameters correspond to high- and low-level policies within a single transformer model and how they are mapped to the model.

The proof of Theorem 4.1 is insufficiently rigorous; it does not establish the claimed equivalence between finding a trajectory from a Lyapunov stable controller and the inference problem, and the logical steps are unclear.
The proof of Theorem 4.3 is overly brief and lacks justification for the initial equation and detailed steps to reach the conclusion.

The experimental results lack statistical analysis; tables are hard to read, no confidence intervals are provided, experiments were run on only three seeds, and unsafe regions in Figure 3 do not align well with hazards, raising doubts about the method's ability to identify unsafe regions.

The connection to Safe RL is weak; the method primarily constrains an offline policy to the data distribution, introduces a tunable hyperparameter D whose use in the algorithm is unclear, and the necessity of the derivation in Section 4 is questionable.

The choice of baselines is suboptimal; comparing only to offline Safe RL algorithms that use cost information directly may be less appropriate than comparing to methods like CQL that also constrain policies within the data distribution.
The writing needs to be polished further.
The Lyapunov condition is not the main contribution, yet it is emphasized, potentially misleading readers about the novelty of the work.
The connection between the proposed Self-Alignment and the original Self-Alignment used in LLMs is unclear.
Experiments are conducted only on several relatively easy safe RL benchmarks.

The evaluation of practical applicability is limited; experiments focus solely on benchmarking environments like Safety Gymnasium and Mujoco, which do not capture real-world complexity and uncertainty.
The paper does not provide information on computational cost or scalability of the framework to more complex or higher-dimensional tasks.
The paper fails to discuss how the SAS framework adapts to environments with unexpected changes or previously unseen safety hazards.
